title: MIP starts from last cycle's plan

blocks.text: 11.2.1 MIP Starts From Last Cycle's Plan

GridCap re-plans its capital portfolio every January. Last January the Ridge region's ten-year plan was solved to optimality and approved. Now 2027 is over: the twelve projects the plan started in 2027 are under way, finance has revised the budgets, the engineers have re-costed some projects, and five new candidates have been added. The planners solve again, and the obvious question is the one lesson 4.3.3 raised: can the solver start from last year's plan instead of from nothing? Lesson 4.3.3 showed *how* to hand MathOpt a hint. This lesson is about *what* to hand it and *whether it helps*: how last cycle's plan becomes a start for this cycle's model, why it usually needs repair first, how each solver reports what it did with it, and how to measure the effect without fooling yourself. GridCap is a fictional utility; its numbers are teaching data.

A **MIP start** (Gurobi's name; MathOpt calls it a solution hint, CP-SAT a hint) is a complete or partial assignment of values to a model's integer variables, given to the solver before it begins. If the solver accepts it as a feasible plan, that plan is its first **incumbent**, the best plan found so far (lesson 3.3.3). A start never changes which plans are allowed or which one is optimal.
The Model

The multi-period timing model of lesson 6.4.1, for one region. One region of a GridCap medium portfolio, about 80 to 110 projects, is small enough to solve to optimality hundreds of times, which is what a benchmark over many runs needs. `plan_model.region_portfolio` keeps one region's projects (a child only if its parent is in the region) and scales each year's budget to the region's share of the portfolio's spend, raised where needed so that every must-do project fits at its earliest start.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the region's projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years, ten of them; $`T_i \subseteq Y`$ the years project $`i`$ may start in; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, with parent $`p(c)`$ and lag $`L_c`$ years.

**Parameters.** $`\text{npv}_{i,t}`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ started in year $`t`$ ($k); $`c_{i,k}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in its $`k`$-th year of work ($k); $`B_y`$, the region's budget in year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$ and $`t \in T_i`$: project $`i`$ starts in year $`t`$.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i} \text{npv}_{i,t}\, x_{i,t}
**Constraints.**

\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall i \in P \setminus M && \text{(once}_i) \\
\sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &= 1 && \forall i \in M && \text{(must}_i) \\
\sum_{i \in g} \sum_{t \in T_i} x_{i,t} &\le 1 && \forall g \in \mathcal{G} && \text{(alt}_g) \\
\sum_{u \in T_c,\, u \le t} x_{c,u} &\le \sum_{s \in T_{p(c)},\, s \le t - L_c} x_{p(c),s} && \forall c \in C,\ t \in T_c && \text{(after}_{c,t}) \\
\sum_{i \in P} \sum_{t \in T_i,\, t \le y} c_{i,\,y-t}\, x_{i,t} &\le B_y && \forall y \in Y && \text{(budget}_y)
\end{aligned}

The code names each row by its label: `once_P017`, `must_P002`, `alt_G006`, `after_P023_2030`, `budget_2029`. The same rows are built three times in `plan_model.py` and `grb_runs.py`, for MathOpt, CP-SAT and gurobipy, because the solvers below are reached through those three APIs.

**Without a Gurobi license.** The Gurobi lines and the Gurobi tables below come from `start_logs.py` and `start_effect_gurobi.py`, and every gurobipy program needs a Gurobi license to start (lesson 5.3.4 explains the kinds of license and how to give the runner yours). Without one, you can read that output but not reproduce it. `start_logs.py` opens its Gurobi environment before it prints anything, so without a license its HiGHS and SCIP lines do not appear either (lesson 5.3.4 shows the error such a program stops with). Everything else in the lesson runs without a license: `roll_forward.py` and `start_effect.py` on HiGHS, `start_effect_scip.py` on SCIP, and all of the lesson's practices.

**This cycle's model** has the same rows over new data: $`Y`$ is the next ten years, $`P`$ loses the projects already committed or whose windows have passed and gains new candidates, each $`T_i`$ loses the year that is over, and $`B_y`$ and some $`c_{i,k}`$ are revised. A **start** is a value $`\hat x_{i,t} \in \{0, 1\}`$ for some or all of this cycle's variables. It is advice to the solver, not a row: nothing above changes when a start is given.
A Plan Rolls Forward One Year, and Its First Year Becomes Fixed

A multi-period model is normally used in a rolling format: solve it, carry out the first period's decisions, and a period later slide the model forward one period with better data and solve again. LINDO's text on multi-period planning (chapter 9) describes exactly this, and the risk that comes with it: the new optimum can differ sharply from the last one, which the people carrying it out find unsettling. `cycles.next_cycle` builds next year's model from this year's portfolio and the approved plan:

The projects the plan started in the year that is over are **committed**: they are being built, so they are no longer decisions, and what they will still spend comes off the later budgets. The horizon loses 2027 and gains 2037. Then the new data arrives, drawn from a seeded random generator so that every run of the course sees the same next cycle: each budget revised by $-3\%$ to $+3\%$, one project in eight re-costed 20% higher (its NPV drops by the extra cost), and five new candidates. A project whose window has passed without a start drops out, and so does a child whose parent can no longer start. A child of a committed parent keeps its lag as an earliest start year:

if parent in committed:                 # the parent started in `first`: the lag is now a date
            earliest, parent, lag = max(earliest, first + p.parent_lag), None, 0
For the Ridge region:

Ridge-2027, cycle 2027-2036: approved plan NPV 50,538, 59 starts, 12 of them in 2027
next cycle 2028-2037: 12 projects committed, 1 dropped, 14 costs revised up 20%, 5 new projects
budgets  2028 2029 2030 2031 2032 ...
  before 7362 7137 7614 9044 12048    (last cycle's, less the committed spend)
  now    7280 6990 7680 8810 12070
model: 90 projects, 192 start variables
Two of the first five budgets went up and three went down, by a few percent. That is a quiet year. It is still enough to make last year's plan illegal, as the next sections show.
Last Cycle's Plan Must Be Mapped Onto This Cycle's Variables

A start is given per variable, and this cycle's variables are not last cycle's. A decision of the old plan, "P031 starts in 2030", carries over only if this cycle's model still has the variable $`x_{P031,2030}`$. Three things can happen to each old decision and each new variable:

items: **kept**: the project is still a decision and its old start year is still in its window, so the start gives that variable 1;
**no variable**: the project is committed (its start year is over) or dropped, so the old decision has nowhere to go;
**new**: a project with no old decision. A complete start gives each of its variables 0, which means "not funded" until the solver finds otherwise.

blocks.text:
allowed = {p.project_id: set(p.starts()) for p in pf.projects}
    carried = {i: t for i, t in old.items() if t in allowed.get(i, ())}
carry forward: kept 47, no variable 12, new 5

Of the plan's 59 starts, 47 still have their variable, and the 12 without one are exactly the 12 committed projects. The new candidates are numbered `N001` to `N005` by `next_cycle`, which is how `carry_forward` tells them apart. The carried plan is still a plan in the data sense, a dict from project to year, and turning it into a **complete** start is one more line: 1 for each variable the plan uses, 0 for every other variable of the model.

Why complete? A **partial** start (values for only some variables, typically only the 1s) leaves the solver to fill in the rest by solving a small MIP of its own, which lesson 4.3.3's HiGHS log showed and which costs work. Gurobi's documentation says the same of its partial MIP starts: completing them means solving subproblems, which can be expensive, and its `StartNodeLimit` parameter caps the nodes spent on it. HiGHS has the same kind of cap, the option `mip_max_start_nodes` (500 nodes by default, per its option list).
<!-- practice 1 -->
Check the Start Against This Cycle's Rows Before Any Solver Sees It

Last year's plan was optimal for last year's data, which means it used nearly every dollar of every budget. This year three of the first five budgets are lower and fourteen projects cost more. Before handing the carried plan to any solver, check it against this cycle's rows. `plan_model.broken` evaluates a plan, as data, against every row of the model and returns the names of the rows it breaks:

carried      NPV  40,005   47 starts  breaks budget_2028, budget_2029, budget_2030, budget_2031, budget_2033, budget_2034, budget_2035, budget_2036
repaired     NPV  36,251   39 starts  breaks nothing
filled       NPV  37,809   55 starts  breaks nothing
greedy       NPV  33,512   58 starts  breaks nothing
optimum      NPV  40,136   47 starts  breaks nothing
The carried plan breaks eight of the ten budget rows. It is not a plan of this cycle's model, and its NPV, 40,005, means nothing. Two steps turn it into one:

items: **Repair**: while a budget row is broken, drop the optional project with the least NPV per $k among those spending in a broken year, and its children with it. Must-do projects are never dropped. Eight projects go, and the plan fits: 36,251.

**Fill**: the repair freed money, and new candidates have none of it yet. Add the projects the plan leaves out, best NPV per $k first, each at its earliest start year that keeps every row (the greedy fill of lesson 3.3.3, now over start years). Sixteen projects come in: 37,809.

blocks.text: The **greedy** row is the same fill run from nothing but the must-do projects: a start that needs no last cycle at all. It is worth 33,512, 16.5% below this cycle's optimum of 40,136; the repaired and filled plan is 5.8% below. Over all eight regions, rolled forward the same way:

cycle        rows the carried plan breaks  filled gap  greedy gap
Ridge-2027                              8       5.80%      16.50%
Valley-2027                             7       3.55%       4.80%
Coast-2027                              9       4.63%      15.96%
Plains-2027                             4       3.79%       6.28%
Ridge-1                                 6       6.69%       9.46%
Valley-1                                7       3.14%      11.26%
Coast-1                                 6       3.38%       1.18%
Plains-1                                7       2.72%       4.32%

Every carried plan breaks between four and nine budget rows. The repaired and filled plan is within 2.7% to 6.7% of the optimum, and it beats the greedy plan on seven of the eight cycles; on Coast-1 the greedy plan is closer. (Names ending in `-2027` and `-1` are the medium portfolios drawn with seeds 2027 and 1.) So the rule: **a plan carried from last cycle is a draft, never a start. Check it against this cycle's rows, repair it, and fill it before any solver sees it.** The next section shows what happens when you skip that.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Each Solver Says in Its Own Words Whether It Took the Start

`start_logs.py` hands four starts to HiGHS and SCIP through MathOpt (lesson 4.3.3's `ModelSolveParameters(solution_hints=[...])`) and to Gurobi through its own API, where a MIP start is the `Start` attribute of each variable:
and keeps only the log lines about the start. The four starts are the carried plan and the repaired-and-filled plan, each given complete (every variable, zeros included) and as its 1s only:

carried, complete: 47 starts given, 192 of 192 variables
  HiGHS   ['User-supplied values of discrete variables cannot yield feasible solution']
  SCIP    nothing about it
  Gurobi  ['User MIP start did not produce a new incumbent solution', 'User MIP start violates constraint budget_2028 by 120.000000000', 'Another try with MIP start']
carried, ones only: 47 starts given, 47 of 192 variables
  HiGHS   ['Attempting to find feasible solution by solving MIP for user-supplied values of 47 / 192 discrete variables']
  SCIP    nothing about it
  Gurobi  ['User MIP start did not produce a new incumbent solution', 'User MIP start violates constraint budget_2028 by 120.000000000']
repaired, complete: 55 starts given, 192 of 192 variables
  HiGHS   ['MIP start solution is feasible, objective value is 37809']
  SCIP    ['1/1 feasible solution given by solution candidate storage, new primal bound 3.780900e+04']
  Gurobi  ['Loaded user MIP start with objective 37809']
repaired, ones only: 55 starts given, 55 of 192 variables
  HiGHS   ['Attempting to find feasible solution by solving MIP for user-supplied values of 55 / 192 discrete variables', 'MIP start solution is feasible, objective value is 37809']
  SCIP    nothing about it
  Gurobi  ['User MIP start produced solution with objective 37809 (<t>s)', 'Loaded user MIP start with objective 37809']
(`<t>` masks a time, which changes on every run.) Read it start by start:

items: **The carried plan, complete.** HiGHS rejects it in one line. Gurobi names the first row it breaks (`budget_2028`, overspent by $120k), tries once more to repair it, and gives up. SCIP says nothing: its log does not show the start at all. None of the three gets a plan out of it, and for HiGHS and SCIP the program checks that the whole run was the one they make with no start at all:

blocks.text:
HiGHS with the carried start, seed 1: the same run as with no start: True
SCIP with the carried start, seed 1: the same run as with no start: True

items: **The carried plan, 1s only.** HiGHS and Gurobi both try to complete it and fail: fixing 47 starts that already overspend 2028 leaves nothing feasible to complete. Leaving out the zeros does not make an infeasible start feasible.
**The repaired plan, complete.** All three accept it as their first incumbent, worth 37,809. This is the only case where every solver's log confirms the start.
**The repaired plan, 1s only.** HiGHS and Gurobi complete it (HiGHS solves a MIP over the 137 variables left free) into the same plan. SCIP's log is silent again.

blocks.text: Gurobi's documentation lists these messages: "Loaded user MIP start" for a start accepted as it is, "User MIP start produced solution" for one it repaired or completed, and "did not produce a new incumbent" for one it discarded. It also separates the MIP start from a **variable hint** (`VarHintVal`, with a confidence `VarHintPri`): a start asks the solver to build one feasible plan from the values, while hints steer heuristics and branching through the whole solve and need not be feasible. MathOpt's `SolutionHint` and CP-SAT's `add_hint` are, despite the name, starts in this sense; lesson 4.6.2 showed CP-SAT trying to repair an infeasible one.

The rule: **only the log, read with and without the start, tells you whether a solver used it** (the MathOpt `SolutionHint` docstring says so too). A silent log, as SCIP's is for three of the four, means you do not know.
A Start Is Measured by the Work to a Good Plan, Over Seeds and Cycles

Does an accepted start make the solve faster? "It found the optimum, and the start was in the log" proves nothing; lesson 5.4.2 showed that one run, or one seed, can show a speed-up that is not there. So the measurement follows lesson 5.4.2's rules:

items: **A fixed instance set, chosen first**: the eight next-cycle models above.
**Several seeds**: 1, 2 and 3, each (cycle, seed) one paired observation, 24 in all.

**Deterministic work, not seconds**: HiGHS and SCIP count LP iterations; Gurobi counts work units (its documentation: very roughly a second, depending on the machine and the model), read here in thousandths. Every run uses one thread.
**Ratios of shifted geometric means**, with the count of observations where the start needed less and more work (W/L).

blocks.text: And one thing lesson 5.4.2 did not need: the work at which each plan was found. A MIP solver reports every new incumbent as it finds it; `runs.py` records each as a pair (work, NPV). SCIP calls a MathOpt callback on `Event.MIP_SOLUTION`, whose `mip_stats` carry the LP iterations so far. (The `callback.py` docstring lists Gurobi and CP-SAT for this event; SCIP calls it too here, and prints two `ERROR` lines on standard error when a callback is registered, while solving normally.) HiGHS ignores MathOpt callbacks (lesson 4.3.5), so its plans are read from its log's progress table, where each row that shows a better `BestSol` is a new plan at `LpIters`. Gurobi's callback reads `GRB.Callback.WORK` at each `MIPSOL`.

From the events, three measures. The **time to first incumbent** is the work at the first event, and "its gap" is how far that plan is below the cycle's optimum. The **work to 1%** is the work at the first plan within 1% of the optimum. The **work to proof** is the whole run's work, with the gap tolerance at 0:

HiGHS
start     to first plan  its gap   to 1%  vs none    W/L  to proof  vs none    W/L
none                  0    80.2%     601     1.00  0/0      15,644     1.00  0/0
repaired              0     4.2%     584     0.97  9/11     15,625     1.00 14/10
greedy                0     8.7%     537     0.89  7/5      15,282     0.98  8/8
(24 paired observations: 8 cycles x 3 seeds; work in LP iterations;
 shifted geometric means, shift 100; W/L: runs with less/more work than with no start)

SCIP
start     to first plan  its gap   to 1%  vs none    W/L  to proof  vs none    W/L
none                  0    24.1%     590     1.00  0/0       8,997     1.00  0/0
repaired              0     4.2%     715     1.21  8/12      7,959     0.88 18/6

Gurobi
start     to first plan  its gap   to 1%  vs none    W/L  to proof  vs none    W/L
none                  0    29.4%       9     1.00  0/0         104     1.00  0/0
carried               0    29.4%       8     0.96 12/10         98     0.94 12/12
repaired              0     4.2%       7     0.84  9/13         98     0.95 11/10
greedy                0     8.7%       7     0.78 12/3         104     1.00 10/6
What the three tables say:

items: **Every solver finds a first plan with almost no work, start or no start.** The time to first incumbent rounds to 0 in every row: before the first LP iteration, the solvers' own trivial heuristics have something. What the start changes is that first plan's quality: 4.2% below the optimum against 80.2% (HiGHS), 24.1% (SCIP) and 29.4% (Gurobi). Measured alone, "time to first incumbent" would call the start useless; measured with the plan's gap, it is the start's whole effect.

**The work to a plan within 1% hardly moves, and can get worse.** HiGHS 0.97 with 9 wins and 11 losses; SCIP 1.21, worse, losing 12 of 20; Gurobi 0.84 but losing 13 of 22. The solvers' own heuristics find plans within 1% within a few hundred LP iterations anyway, and a start changes the search's path, which can delay them.

**The work to proof is about the same.** SCIP's 0.88 (18 wins, 6 losses) is the one consistent gain; HiGHS's 1.00 and Gurobi's 0.95 are noise-sized. Proving optimality means pushing the bound down to the optimum (lesson 3.4.1), and a start does nothing for the bound.

**The carried, infeasible start changed Gurobi's path** (its rows differ from "none") without ever becoming a plan; HiGHS and SCIP dropped it, so it is not in their tables (`start_logs.py` shows why).

blocks.text: So the common advice is right that a good start gives the solver an incumbent at once, and so a bound to prune with; on these models that did not translate into a faster proof, except a 12% saving for SCIP. Measure it on your own models before promising it.
<!-- practice 3 -->
A Start Is Insurance for a Solve That Is Stopped Early

If the start barely speeds up the proof, why give one? Because real solves are stopped: by a time or work limit, by a gap target, by the night ending. A stopped solve returns the best plan it has. The second half of each program asks what that plan is worth after a fixed amount of work: the mean gap, over the 24 observations, of the best plan found within that much work.

mean gap of the best plan in hand, by work done (LP iterations):
start             0        50       200      1000
none         46.89%    24.43%    15.10%     0.55%
repaired      4.18%     4.18%     4.18%     0.46%
greedy        7.75%     6.94%     6.76%     0.51%
repaired start, seed 1, solved again: every run repeated: True

mean gap of the best plan in hand, by work done (LP iterations):
start             0        50       200      1000
none         22.64%    15.24%     3.28%     0.35%
repaired      4.21%     4.21%     3.40%     0.50%
repaired start, seed 1, solved again: every run repeated: True

mean gap of the best plan in hand, by work done (thousandths of a work unit):
start             0         1         5        20
none        no plan    29.30%     1.19%     0.46%
carried     no plan    29.30%     1.34%     0.45%
repaired      4.21%     4.17%     1.50%     0.38%
greedy        8.72%     8.68%     1.09%     0.41%
repaired start, seed 1, solved again: every run repeated: True

The tables are HiGHS, SCIP and Gurobi, in that order. At zero work the plan in hand can be better than the first plan of the tables above, because a solver may find several plans before its first LP iteration and keeps the best. Stopped after 50 LP iterations, HiGHS without a start hands back a plan 24% below the optimum on average; with the repaired start, 4.2%. Gurobi stopped at zero work has no plan at all without a start. By 1,000 LP iterations (or 20 thousandths of a Gurobi work unit) every row is within about half a percent, and the start's advantage is gone; SCIP's and Gurobi's repaired rows are even slightly behind there. The last line of each program solves the eight repaired-start runs of seed 1 again and checks that every number repeated, so these tables can be quoted.

That is what a start buys: **a floor under the plan a stopped solve returns, at no cost to the answer of a solve that finishes.** It is worth most when solves are stopped early, which is the normal case for large models such as the 10,000-project portfolio of lesson 11.1.3, and inside the heuristics of lesson 11.3.5. And because the greedy plan, which needs no last cycle, gives most of the same floor, a new model with no history can still start from something.
Summary

items: **A plan rolls forward one year, and its first year becomes fixed.** Committed projects leave the decisions and their remaining spend leaves the budgets; the horizon slides one year.
**Last cycle's plan must be mapped onto this cycle's variables.** Keep a decision where its variable still exists, drop it where it does not, give new projects 0, and hand over a complete start.
**Check the start against this cycle's rows before any solver sees it.** Every carried plan broke four to nine budget rows; repaired and filled, it came within 2.7% to 6.7% of the optimum.

**Each solver says in its own words whether it took the start.** HiGHS, SCIP and Gurobi all logged the repaired complete start; the carried one was rejected or silently dropped; SCIP's log was silent on three of the four starts.

**A start is measured by the work to a good plan, over seeds and cycles.** On 24 paired runs the start cut the first plan's gap from 24% to 80% down to 4.2%, barely changed the work to 1%, and saved 12% of the proof only for SCIP.
**A start is insurance for a solve that is stopped early.** After 50 HiGHS LP iterations the plan in hand was 4.2% from optimal with the start and 24% without; by 1,000 the difference was gone.

blocks.text: **Further reading:** [MathOpt (OR-Tools)](https://developers.google.com/optimization/math_opt) (warm starts by solution or by basis among MathOpt's features); the `SolutionHint` and `ModelSolveParameters` docstrings in [`model_parameters.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/model_parameters.py) (partial and infeasible hints completed by a sub-MIP, the first hint used by a solver that takes one, and reading the log with and without the hint); the `Event.MIP_SOLUTION` and `CallbackData` docstrings in [`callback.py`](https://github.com/google/or-tools/blob/stable/ortools/math_opt/python/callback.py) (an event per new incumbent, `mip_stats` filled on it); Gurobi, [Warm Start Options](https://docs.gurobi.com/projects/optimizer/en/13.0/features/warmstart.html) (the `Start` attribute, partial and infeasible starts, `StartNodeLimit`, `NumStart` and `StartNumber`, variable hints against MIP starts, and the log messages above); HiGHS, [option definitions](https://ergo-code.github.io/HiGHS/dev/options/definitions/) (`mip_max_start_nodes`, the node limit for completing a partial start); [LINDO, Multi-period Planning Problems, chapter 9](https://www.lindo.com/downloads/LINGO_text/Chapter9.pdf) (section 9.1: multi-period models used in a rolling format, and the "nervousness" of plans that change sharply between periods).
Challenges

items: Raise the budget revision in `next_cycle` to $`\pm 10\%`$. Predict whether the carried plan breaks more rows, and whether the repaired start's gap grows.
Hand Gurobi two starts, the carried plan as start 0 and the repaired plan as start 1 (`NumStart = 2`, then `StartNumber` before each set of `Start` values). Predict which log lines appear.
A planner wants this year's plan to change as little as possible from last year's. Is a start the tool for that? (Look at what a start promises about the final plan.)
Stop every solve at 200 LP iterations instead of running to proof. Which column of the tables would you report to the planners, and why?

blocks.text: Design Note: A Start Is Data You Can Test

`start_effect.py` never hands a solver a start it has not first checked with `broken`, and `starts.py` works only on plans as dicts. That keeps the expensive question ("does it help?") separate from the cheap one ("is it a plan?"). The cheap one runs in microseconds, needs no solver, and catches the mistake that cost every carried start here its value. Write the repair and the check as plain functions with tests, as the practices do, and the solver only ever sees starts that are plans.
The Full Programs

Each snippet above is part of a complete program, and each program printed the output the lesson shows. Open one to read it whole, change it, and run it again: Run starts the program on your copy of the code, so the course's own files never change. The Gurobi programs need a Gurobi license (lesson 5.3.4); the free size-limited one is enough.

**roll_forward.py.** Rolls the Ridge region's approved plan forward one cycle, carries it into the new model, checks, repairs and fills it, and compares it with a greedy plan and the optimum on all eight regions (*A Plan Rolls Forward*, *Last Cycle's Plan Must Be Mapped*, *Check the Start*). *Try:* Change the seed of `next_cycle` from 7 to 8 and predict whether the carried plan still breaks most budget rows.

**start_logs.py.** Four starts, each handed to HiGHS, SCIP and Gurobi, with the log lines about the start (*Each Solver Says in Its Own Words*). *Try:* Give only the starts in 2028 and predict HiGHS's "k / n" numbers.

**start_effect.py, start_effect_scip.py, start_effect_gurobi.py.** Every cycle, seed and kind of start, compared pairwise with no start, then the plan in hand after fixed amounts of work (*A Start Is Measured*, *A Start Is Insurance*). *Try:* Add 0.5% to the measures by changing `within(..., 0.01)` to `0.005` in `start_bench.py`, and predict whether the start helps more at the tighter target.
